# 2.4 – The Distributive Property {.unnumbered}

Imagine your football (soccer) team wants to order new jerseys. Each jersey costs \$25, and to add your team’s logo it’s another \$5 per jersey.

Since there are 11 players on the team, you need 11 jerseys. You could figure out the total cost in two different ways:

First, add the cost of one jersey and the logo: 25 + 5 = 30. Then multiply by 11 → 11 × 30 = \$330.

Or multiply separately: (11 × 25) + (11 × 5) = 275 + 55 = \$330.

Either way, you get the same answer. What we just did actually followed a rule in algebra called the {{< glink distributive property >}}. Today, we’re going to see how this property helps us simplify expressions.

---

::: objectives
- [ ] I can use the **distributive property** to expand expressions like $a(b+c)$.
- [ ] I can distribute with **negatives** and then **combine like terms**.
- [ ] I can **factor out** a common factor (reverse distribution) to rewrite an expression.
:::

---

::: vocab
{{< glink distributive property >}}, {{< glink equivalent expressions >}}, {{< glink expand >}}, {{< glink simplify >}}
:::

## 👥 Learn Together

---

### 2.4.1 – What Is the Distributive Property?

At the beginning of Algebra class, your teacher hands you a stack of worksheets and says, *“Please distribute these to the class.”*  

To **distribute** the worksheets, you hand one to each student.  

In math, distribution works the same way. When we multiply an expression by a number, we "give" that number to each term in the expression.

The {{< glink distributive property >}} says:

$$
a(b+c) = ab + ac \qquad\text{and}\qquad a(b-c) = ab - ac
$$

---

**Example:**

{{< glink Expand >}} $3(x + 2)$ using the distributive property.

To do this, distribute the 3. That is, multiply each term in $(x+2)$ by 3:

```{=html}
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="720" height="110" viewBox="0 0 720 110"
     style="display:block; margin:0 auto; font-family:'Times New Roman',serif">
  <defs>
    <marker id="arrow" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" refX="4.5" refY="2.5" orient="auto">
      <polygon points="0 0, 5 2.5, 0 5" fill="currentColor"></polygon>
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <!-- 3(x+2) -->
  <text x="15"  y="75" font-size="16pt">3</text>
  <text x="35"  y="75" font-size="16pt">(</text>
  <text x="45"  y="75" font-size="16pt">x</text>
  <text x="70"  y="75" font-size="16pt">+</text>
  <text x="100" y="75" font-size="16pt">2</text>
  <text x="115" y="75" font-size="16pt">)</text>

  <!-- rainbow arcs -->
  <path d="M 20 50 C 30 35, 50 35, 52 55"
        stroke="crimson" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#arrow)"></path>
  <path d="M 20 50 C 38 20, 105 25, 105 55"
        stroke="steelblue" stroke-width="2" fill="none" marker-end="url(#arrow)"></path>

  <!-- result -->
  <text x="140" y="75" font-size="16pt">=</text>
  <text x="170" y="75" font-size="16pt">3x + 6</text>
</svg>
```

---

We can also see this with **algebra tiles**. The expression $x + 2$ looks like:

![](/images/Unit_2/Lesson_4/x_plus_2.png){width="40%" fig-align="center"}

Multiplying by 3 means taking 3 groups of $(x+2)$:

![](/images/Unit_2/Lesson_4/x_plus_2_times_3.png){width="40%" fig-align="center"}

If we count the tiles, there are 3 $x$’s and 6 ones.
In other words: **$3x + 6$**.

:::{.gotcha title="Don't skip a term!"}
When you distribute make sure you multiply **every** term in the expression. Students often make the mistake of only distributing to the first term.

**Example:**

$$
4(x + 2y + 5) = 4(x) + 4(2y) + 4(5) = 4x + 8y + 20
$$

:::

::: {.you-try title="Expand $5(x+7)$ using the distributive property."}
$$
5(x+7) = 5(x) + 5(7) = 5x + 35
$$

:::


---

### 2.4.2 – Distributing with Negatives

Distribution with negatives is no different than what we have seen so far. But you need to be careful! It is easy to forget to include the negative sign when applying the distributive property.

**Example 1:**

Expand the expression $-3(x - 4)$:

$$
-3(x - 4) = -3(x) -3(-4) = -3x + 12
$$

**Example 2:**

Expand the expression $-(2x - 7)$:

$$
-(2x - 7) = -1(2x - 7) = -2x + 7
$$


::: {.you-try title="Expand $-2(3-y)$"}
$$
-2(3 - y) = -2(3) - 2(-y) = -6 + 2y
$$
:::

---

### 2.4.3 – Distribute, Then Combine Like Terms

Expanding an expression using the distributive property often requires us to simplify the result. To do this, we combine like terms like we did in the previous lesson.

**Example:**

Simplify the expression $4(x+2) + 3(x-5)$:

First we expand using the distributive property.
$$
4(x+2) + 3(x-5) = 4x + 8 + 3x - 15 
$$

Then we simplify by combining like terms:

$$
4x + 8 + 3x - 15 = 7x - 7
$$

:::{.callout-tip title="Make it simpler"}
When possible, you should simplify what is inside the parentheses before distributing.

**Example:**

$$
2(3x - 2y + 5 - x + 5y - 10) = 2(8x + 3y - 5) = 16x + 6y - 10
$$
:::

::: {.gotcha title="Watch those signs!"}
Students often forget to keep the sign with the muliplier.

**Example:**

Simplify the following expression:

$$
3(x - 2) - 5(4x + 5)
$$

Notice the "-" sign in front of the 5. We **must** multiply the second part of the expression by -5.

$$
3(x - 2) \color{red}- 5\color{black}(4x + 5) = 3x - 6 \color{red}-20x - 25 \color{black} = -17x - 31
$$

:::

---

### 2.4.4 – Reverse It: Factoring Out a Common Factor

Distribution goes both ways. If $ab+ac = a(b+c)$, then we can **factor out** $a$.

**Examples**

1.  $8x+12 = 4(2x+3)$
2.  $15x-9 = 3(5x-3)$
3.  $3x+6y = 3(x+2y)$

This is called **factoring** (using a **greatest common factor**, if possible).

::: {.you-try-m title="Factor the expression (reverse distribute)."}
a)  $12x+18$    b) $9a-6$    c) $14y+21x$    d) $15x-9x^2$
:::

::: {.answer title="Answer"}
a)  $6(2x+3)$    b) $3(3a-2)$    c) $7(2y+3x)$    d) $3x(5-3x)$
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.4.5 – Check Your Work

Use a quick **substitution** to confirm equivalence.

Example: Is $5(2x-3)-(x-4)$ the same as $9x-11$?

Expand: $5(2x-3)-(x-4)=10x-15-x+4=9x-11.$

Check $x=2$: $5(4-3)-(2-4)=5(1)-(-2)=5+2=7 \quad \text{and} \quad 9(2)-11=18-11=7.$ They match.

::: {.gotcha title="Important: Exponents don’t distribute over addition"}
$(x+2)^2 \neq x^2+2^2$. Correct: $(x+2)^2=(x+2)(x+2)=x^2+4x+4$.
:::

## 🏋️ Practice On Your Own

**Expand using the distributive property**

1.  $6(x+5)$
2.  $7(y-2)$
3.  $4(3a+b)$
4.  $10(m+0.3)$
5.  $-3(p+9)$
6.  $-(k-8)$

**Expand, then combine like terms**

7.  $2(x+3)+5(x-1)$
8.  $4y-2(3y-7)$
9.  $3(a+2b)-5(2a-b)$
10. $-2(t-5)+3(t+1)$

**With decimals and fractions**

11. $0.5(8x-6)$
12. $1.2(y+5)-0.2y$
13. $\dfrac{3}{4}(4x-8)$
14. $-\dfrac{1}{2}(6a+10)$

**Factor (reverse distribute)**

15. $18x+27$
16. $20m-12$
17. $8p+12q$
18. $14x-21x^2$

**Are they equivalent? Expand/simplify and compare.**

19. $3(x+4)+2x$ and $5x+12$
20. $6-2(x+3)$ and $-2x$
21. $5(a-1)+a$ and $6a-5$
22. $4(y+2)-3(y-1)$ and $y+11$

**Challenge Problems**

23. Show two different ways to simplify $3(x+5)-2(x-1)$ (e.g., distribute-first vs. combine-inside-first if possible). Explain why both give the same result.

24. Create **two equivalent expressions** that look different: one using parentheses and one fully expanded. Explain how you know they’re equivalent.

**Expand using the distributive property**

1.  $6x+30$
2.  $7y-14$
3.  $12a+4b$
4.  $10m+3$
5.  $-3p-27$
6.  $-k+8$

7.  $2x+6+5x-5=7x+1$
8.  $4y-6y+14=-2y+14$
9.  $3a+6b-10a+5b=-7a+11b$
10. $-2t+10+3t+3 = t+13$

**With decimals and fractions**

11. $4x-3$
12. $1.2y+6-0.2y = 1.0y+6$ or $y+6$
13. $3x-6$
14. $-3a-5$

**Factor (reverse distribute)**

15. $9(2x+3)$
16. $4(5m-3)$
17. $4(2p+3q)$
18. $7x(2-3x)$

**Are they equivalent?**

19. yes (both $5x+12$)
20. yes (both $-2x$)
21. yes (both $6a-5$)
22. yes (both $y+11$)
:::
